# Learning Games {#sec-games}

Some ideas only click when you try them yourself. Each game here takes 10 to 20 minutes and runs in your web browser on a laptop or phone. Every game follows the same pattern:

1. **Read the goal.** The intro screen tells you what you'll learn.
2. **Play a level.** Levels start small and get harder. Each round is randomly generated, so you can replay as often as you like.
3. **Compare.** The results screen puts your answer next to a benchmark, such as a classic heuristic or the true optimum.
4. **Debrief.** A short explanation connects what happened to the chapter, with the formulas worked out using your numbers.

::: {.callout-tip title="Playing in class"}
The results screen shows a **seed** number. Add `?level=2&seed=12345` to a game's address and everyone gets exactly the same round, so a whole class can compete on one puzzle and then compare answers.
:::

## Line Balancer

[Production]{.pill} [10 to 15 min]{.pill} [Week 5](chapters/week-05.qmd)

**You will learn to** compute [takt time]{.term} from demand, assign tasks to [workstations]{.term key="workstation"} without breaking the [precedence diagram]{.term}, and judge a line by its number of stations, [cycle time]{.term}, and [balance delay]{.term}.

Drag tasks onto stations (or tap a task, then a station) until every station fits within the takt time. When you submit, you'll see your line next to the largest-candidate rule, the ranked positional weight method, and the exact optimum.

[Play Line Balancer](games/line-balancer/index.html){.btn .btn-primary} [Read Week 5](chapters/week-05.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}

## Spot the Shift

[Quality control]{.pill} [10 to 15 min]{.pill} [Week 7](chapters/week-07.qmd)

**You will learn to** read an X-bar and R [control chart]{.term}, use [control limits]{.term key="control-limits"} and the [Western Electric rules]{.term} to spot a process change, and weigh a [Type I error]{.term} (false alarm) against a [Type II error]{.term} (late detection).

A bottle-filling line streams live samples. At a hidden moment the process jumps, spreads out, or drifts. Stop the line too early and you pay for a false alarm. Stop too late and you pay for scrap. Afterwards you'll see exactly when each rule would have fired and learn about [average run length]{.term}.

[Play Spot the Shift](games/spot-the-shift/index.html){.btn .btn-primary} [Read Week 7](chapters/week-07.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}

## Lift Lab

[Ergonomics]{.pill} [10 to 15 min]{.pill} [Week 6](chapters/week-06.qmd)

**You will learn to** read the six multipliers of the [NIOSH lifting equation]{.term}, find the one that hurts a lifting job most, and bring the job's [Lifting Index]{.term} to 1 or less for the least money.

A worker lifts boxes from a pallet to a shelf, and the job is unsafe. Bring the load closer, change the heights, remove the twist, slow the pace, or improve the grip, and watch the [recommended weight limit]{.term} change as you go. Every change costs money. The results screen shows the cheapest redesign that works. The equation and its tables come from the NIOSH applications manual [@waters1994niosh].

[Play Lift Lab](games/lift-lab/index.html){.btn .btn-primary} [Read Week 6](chapters/week-06.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}

## Build for Uptime

[Reliability]{.pill} [10 to 15 min]{.pill} [Week 4](chapters/week-04.qmd)

**You will learn to** compute the [reliability]{.term} of parts in a [series system]{.term} and a [parallel system]{.term}, decide where [redundancy]{.term} is worth its cost, and check a calculation against simulated missions.

Build an irrigation system from a shelf of parts. Each part has a reliability and a price, and you can add spares in parallel. Stay within budget, then run 200 missions (a [Monte Carlo simulation]{.term}) and count the failures. The results screen shows the most reliable design the budget allows.

[Play Build for Uptime](games/build-for-uptime/index.html){.btn .btn-primary} [Read Week 4](chapters/week-04.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}

## Order Chain

[Supply chain]{.pill} [10 to 20 min]{.pill} [Week 9](chapters/week-09.qmd)

**You will learn to** explain how delays and local information turn a small change in demand into large order swings, called the [bullwhip effect]{.term}, and how sharing demand information reduces them.

Run one stage of a four-stage bicycle helmet [supply chain]{.term}: retailer, wholesaler, distributor, or factory. Place one order a week while automated players run the other three stages, or pass one device around a team of four. Afterwards you'll see everyone's orders, [inventory]{.term}, and every [backorder]{.term}, next to the same weeks played with a [base-stock policy]{.term} and shared demand information.

[Play Order Chain](games/order-chain/index.html){.btn .btn-primary} [Read Week 9](chapters/week-09.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}

## About the games

- **Private.** The games run entirely in your browser. Nothing you do is sent anywhere. Your best score per level is kept only on your device.
- **Accessible.** Every game works with a keyboard, uses a color-blind-safe palette, and follows the book's light or dark mode.
- **More on the way.** Games on routing, linear programming, safe lifting, engineering economics, project crashing, supply chains, reliability, queueing, and machine learning are planned for later chapters.
